query: Consider the following context: How to rationally design composition of alloys with desired properties has always been an open and challenging question, especially for high-entropy alloy (HEA) which has huge selections of composition due to the feature of multi-principal elements. Although great efforts have been made in the past decades, such as approaches based on thermo-kinetic analysis and simulations, strategies to quick determine the optimal HEA composition remain lacking. In that context, which method can be used for design intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight refractory HEA (RHEA) compositions, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an active learning algorithm with high-throughput experimental feedback can rapidly identify RHEA compositions that are intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight, outperforming compositions designed via traditional thermo-kinetic or simulation-based methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline refractory high-entropy alloys designed using conventional thermo-kinetic analysis and simulation, with a broad composition range of multi-principal refractory elements.
generation.intervention: Apply a closed-loop, data-driven framework where an active learning algorithm iteratively suggests new alloy compositions based on high-throughput synthesis and rapid property characterization.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under refractory conditions with rapid thermal processing (e.g., ~1200°C) and short processing times (minutes to hours); alloy compositions varied within defined atomic percentage ranges (e.g., 5%–40%).
generation.structural_mediator: Microstructural features such as phase distribution and grain size, which evolve as a function of alloy composition and processing conditions, mediate the mechanical properties.
generation.mechanism: Real-time experimental feedback refines the ML algorithm’s training data, progressively narrowing the search space toward alloy compositions that optimize strength, ductility, and low weight. This iterative process minimizes computational load while honing in on predictive composition-property relationships.
generation.predicted_outcome: The active learning-driven design approach will yield RHEA compositions with significantly improved mechanical performance compared to baseline alloys, exhibiting a favorable combination of strength, ductility, and low weight.
generation.baseline: Conventional RHEA compositions determined solely via traditional thermo-kinetic analysis and simulation without iterative experimental feedback.
generation.boundary: The improvements are anticipated under the specified rapid processing and testing conditions; results may not generalize to different processing regimes or non-refractory alloy systems.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of performance enhancement and the exact compositional parameters remain uncertain until sufficient high-throughput experimental data is collected to robustly train the ML model.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel experiments comparing RHEA compositions obtained through the active learning framework against those designed by conventional methods. Use high-throughput synthesis to generate compositions, coupled with rapid thermal processing and subsequent mechanical property testing.
measurements: Strength (e.g., yield and ultimate tensile strength)
Microstructural analysis (e.g., phase identification, grain size)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RHEA compositions optimized via active learning do not show statistically significant improvements in strength, ductility, and low weight compared to the conventionally designed compositions under identical test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

levers.lever: Active Learning with High-Throughput Experimental Feedback
levers.principle: This approach uses a closed-loop data-driven framework where machine learning algorithms suggest new alloy compositions based on high-throughput synthesis and rapid property characterization. Key parameters include alloy composition ranges (e.g., element atomic percentages varied between 5% and 40%), synthesis temperatures (e.g., rapid thermal processing around 1200°C), and short processing times (minutes to hours). It overcomes the limitation by iteratively refining the training data set with real-time experimental feedback, drastically reducing the search space and computational load.

levers.lever: Bayesian Optimization Incorporating Gaussian Process Surrogates
levers.principle: Leveraging Bayesian optimization, the method employs Gaussian Process models to predict performance metrics (strength, ductility, density) based on compositional features. Key parameters include defined search boundaries for element concentrations (e.g., 10–50 at.%), process temperature settings (e.g., refractory conditions >1000°C), and simulation-to-experiment transfer times (on the order of hours per iteration). It addresses the open question by efficiently navigating the vast compositional space to quickly identify promising candidates with the desired balance of properties.

This lever uses pre-trained models on large thermodynamic and kinetic simulation databases to predict properties of unexplored HEA compositions. By fine-tuning these models with limited high-quality experimental data, key parameters such as element-specific mixing enthalpy (optimized within ±5 kJ/mol margins) and operating temperature ranges (e.g., 1000°C to 1400°C) are used. It accelerates the design process by capitalizing on existing knowledge, significantly reducing simulation expenses and experimental trial numbers.

levers.lever: Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Objective Composition Optimization
levers.principle: Using reinforcement learning (RL), this method formulates the alloy design as a sequential decision-making problem with rewards based on meeting targets for strength, ductility, and low density under high-temperature environments. Key settings include reward functions calibrated with experimentally measured mechanical properties (target tensile strength >1 GPa, ductility >10% elongation) and operational refractory conditions (temperatures above 1000°C). The RL agent continuously adjusts design variables (composition, processing time, and temperature profiles), thus effectively circumventing the slow convergence of traditional simulations.
